line: e4 c5 f4 d5 e5 Bf5
teaches: When a closed centre is coming and you will need a pawn on e6, develop the light-squared bishop FIRST. That one move is the difference between an active piece and the bad bishop that defines every version of this structure — and it is available for exactly one move, before the pawn goes.
explains: The bishop steps outside the chain to f5, hitting the pawn on c2 down the open diagonal. Once the e-pawn advances behind it, this bishop is already on the good side of everything.

line: e4 c5 f4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Qb6
teaches: When a bishop is lining up to trade itself for your knight and wreck your pawns, the answer is not to move the knight — it is to arrange a recapture by a PIECE. The trade then still happens, and it costs you nothing: they have spent a bishop to develop your queen.
explains: The queen steps to b6 defending the knight on c6, so the exchange on that square is answered by the queen rather than by a pawn. The structure stays whole and the queen is developed to an active square in the same move.
